prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

THE NIGHT THAT LORCA COMES SHALL BE A STRANGE NIGHT IN THE SOUTH, IT SHALL BE THE TIME WHEN NEGROES LEAVE THE SOUTH FOREVER, GREEN TRAINS SHALL ARRIVE FROM RED PLANET MARS CRACKLING BLUENESS SHALL SEND TOOTH-COVERED CARS FOR THEM TO LEAVE IN, TO GO INTO THE NORTH FOREVER, AND I SEE MY LITTLE GIRL MOTHER AGAIN WITH HER CROSS THAT IS NOT BURNING, HER SKIRTS OF BLACK, OF ALL COLORS, HER AURA OF FAMILIARITY. THE SOUTH SHALL WEEP BITTER TEARS TO NO AVAIL, THE NEGROES HAVE GONE INTO CRACKLING BLUENESS. CRISPUS ATTUCKS SHALL ARRIVE WITH THE BOSTON COMMONS, TO TAKE ELISSI LANDI NORTH, CRISPUS ATTUCKS SHALL BE LAYING ON BOSTON COMMONS, ELISSI LANDI SHALL FEEL ALIVE AGAIN. I SHALL CALL HER NAME AS SHE STEPS ON TO THE BOSTON COMMONS, AND FLIES NORTH FOREVER, LINCOLN SHALL BE THERE, TO SEE THEM LEAVE THE SOUTH FOREVER, ELISSI LANDI, SHE WILL BE GREEN. THE WHITE SOUTH SHALL GATHER AT PRESERVATION HALL.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: THE, NIGHT, THAT

outputs.L1:
The night that Lorca comes shall be a strange night in the South. It shall be the time when Negroes leave the South forever. Green trains shall arrive from the red planet Mars; crackling blueness shall send tooth-covered cars for them to depart in, to go into the North forever. And I shall see my little-girl mother again, with her cross that is not burning, her skirts of black, of all colors, her aura of familiarity.

The South shall weep bitter tears to no avail; the Negroes have gone into crackling blueness. Crispus Attucks shall arrive with the Boston Commons to take Elissi Landi north. Crispus Attucks shall be lying on Boston Commons; Elissi Landi shall feel alive again. I shall call her name as she steps onto the Boston Commons and flies north forever. Lincoln shall be there to see them leave the South forever. Elissi Landi—she will be green.

The white South shall gather at Preservation Hall.
outputs.L2:
On the night Lorca arrives, the South will be filled with strangeness. It will be the hour when Black people depart from the South for good. Green trains will come from the red planet Mars, and the crackling blue will dispatch cars covered in teeth to carry them away, carrying them north forever. Then I will see my mother as a little girl once more, holding her cross that is not aflame, wearing skirts that are black and every color, surrounded by the feeling of someone known and close.

The South will cry with bitter sorrow, but its grief will change nothing; the Black people will have vanished into the crackling blue. Crispus Attucks will come bearing Boston Commons, arriving to bring Elissi Landi north. Crispus Attucks will lie upon Boston Commons, and Elissi Landi will feel herself living again. I will speak her name as she steps onto Boston Commons and flies north without return. Lincoln will stand there too, watching them leave the South forever. Elissi Landi—she will be green. The white South will assemble at Preservation Hall.
outputs.L3:
The speaker imagines a strange, apocalyptic night when Black people leave the South forever. This departure is not described as an ordinary migration, but as a dramatic, almost supernatural event. The night feels charged with mystery and finality, as if history itself has reached a turning point. The South, long associated with oppression, violence, and racial suffering, is abandoned completely.

The imagery used to describe this escape is surreal and dreamlike. Green trains, Mars, and “crackling blueness” create a sense of movement beyond the limits of ordinary reality. These images suggest that liberation is not only a physical journey away from the South, but also a transformation into another world. The trains may represent mass departure, while Mars and the strange blue atmosphere evoke distance, freedom, and the possibility of a radically different future.

After Black people have gone, the South is imagined as weeping helplessly. This reversal is important: a region that once depended on Black labor while denying Black humanity is now left powerless and grief-stricken. Its tears suggest regret, loss, and perhaps fear. Without the people it exploited, the South becomes empty and broken, forced to confront what it has done and what it has lost.

Historical figures such as Crispus Attucks and Abraham Lincoln appear as witnesses or guides in this vision of liberation. Their presence connects the imagined exodus to a longer history of struggle, sacrifice, and freedom. Attucks, often remembered as one of the first martyrs of the American Revolution, symbolizes Black participation in the fight for liberty from the nation’s beginning. Lincoln, associated with emancipation, represents another crucial moment in the history of Black freedom. Together, these figures give the vision a historical and symbolic weight.

Elissi Landi is portrayed as coming alive again and flying north forever. Her resurrection and flight intensify the poem’s atmosphere of fantasy and transformation. She becomes part of the larger movement away from the South, carried into a future that is free, distant, and irreversible. Through this image, the speaker suggests not only escape from oppression, but also rebirth: the possibility that those who were silenced, trapped, or destroyed can rise again and move toward freedom.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a surreal and prophetic vision of a mass exodus of Black people from the American South. Rather than describing migration in ordinary historical terms, it imagines departure as a vast, almost supernatural event. Black people rise up and leave the South together, transforming the landscape and overturning the social order that had depended on their labor, suffering, and subjugation. The movement becomes more than physical relocation: it is a symbolic escape from racial terror, economic exploitation, and the long legacy of slavery.

The imagery is visionary and dreamlike. Historical figures, spiritual symbols, and strange transformations appear together, giving the scene the force of prophecy. The South is not simply a place on a map, but a region haunted by violence, bondage, and injustice. As Black people depart, the old world loses its foundation. The society that claimed dominance over them is revealed to be helpless without them. Its power collapses into grief, confusion, and emptiness.

The most important result of this imagined exodus is the South’s powerless sorrow as Black people leave “forever” for a freer North. Their departure is not temporary, and it is not presented as a request for permission or reform. It is final. The South can only mourn what it has lost, while those who leave move toward a space associated with freedom, possibility, and self-determination.

In this way, the text turns migration into an act of historical justice. It reimagines liberation not as something granted by oppressors, but as something seized collectively by the oppressed. The exodus becomes both a flight from racial violence and a radical rewriting of history, in which Black people abandon the world that abused them and create the possibility of a new future beyond its control.
outputs.L5:
**The Night That Changed Everything**

The night that the storm arrived, the whole town seemed to hold its breath. Rain tapped against the windows like impatient fingers, and the wind moved through the streets with a low, restless voice. Everyone stayed inside, wrapped in blankets and silence, waiting for morning.

But for one young girl named Mara, that night was different. She saw a small light flickering near the old bridge, where no one should have been. Though she was afraid, she put on her coat, took a lantern, and stepped into the rain.

What she found there changed everything: a lost traveler, injured and alone, calling softly for help. Mara ran back for the villagers, and together they brought the stranger to safety.

By morning, the storm had passed. The town was quiet again, washed clean by rain. But everyone remembered the night that Mara had been brave—the night that turned fear into courage and a stranger into a friend.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, prophetic prose poem in all caps about the American South, the Great Migration, Lorca, Crispus Attucks, Lincoln, Mars, and Preservation Hall.
counterfactuals.output:
THE SOUTH DREAMS IN RED CLAY AND CHURCH FANS, IN MOSQUITO SONG AND RAILROAD IRON, IN THE SWEAT OF COTTON FIELDS WHERE THE MOON HANGS LIKE A BROKEN PLATE OVER THE PINES. SHE SPEAKS THROUGH HER DEAD WITH A MOUTH FULL OF MAGNOLIAS. SHE SAYS: CHILDREN, THE TRAIN IS COMING, AND IT HAS ALWAYS BEEN COMING.

AND THE PEOPLE RISE NORTHWARD LIKE PSALMS OF SMOKE, LIKE BLACKBIRDS UNSTITCHING THE SKY FROM MISSISSIPPI TO CHICAGO, FROM ALABAMA TO DETROIT, FROM NEW ORLEANS TO HARLEM, CARRYING SKILLETS, BIBLES, TRUMPETS, NAMES. THE GREAT MIGRATION IS NOT A ROAD BUT A CONSTELLATION; EVERY FOOTSTEP A STAR, EVERY STATION A WOUND THAT LEARNS TO SING.

LORCA WALKS BESIDE THEM IN A GREEN SUIT OF RAIN, WEEPING GYPSY VERSES INTO A PAPER BAG, SAYING THE DUENDE LIVES WHERE THE KNIFE ENTERS THE SONG. HE SEES THE SOUTH AS A BLACK HORSE DRINKING FROM A WELL OF FIRE. HE SEES THE RIVER TURN TO INK. HE SEES THE LYNCHING TREE BLOSSOM WITH EYES. HE SEES, AND HIS VISION IS A GUITAR STRUNG WITH HUMAN HAIR.

CRISPUS ATTUCKS STANDS AT THE CROSSROADS, FIRST BLOOD BECOME THUNDER, HIS CHEST A DOOR NO EMPIRE CAN CLOSE. HE LIFTS HIS HAND AND THE BULLETS BECOME SEEDS. FROM THEM GROW CITIES, BRASS BANDS, BARBERSHOPS, STRIKE LINES, MOTHERS CALLING CHILDREN HOME BEFORE DARK. HE SAYS: LIBERTY IS A DRUM THAT BEGINS IN THE BODY.

LINCOLN RISES FROM HIS MARBLE CHAIR WITH MUD ON HIS BOOTS AND A MOTH IN HIS BEARD. HE DOES NOT SPEAK IN MONUMENTS NOW. HE SPEAKS IN RAIL SPIKES, IN TORN CONTRACTS, IN THE LOW CREAK OF HISTORY TURNING OVER IN ITS SLEEP. HIS SHADOW IS LONG ENOUGH TO COVER A FIELD, BUT NOT LONG ENOUGH TO HEAL IT. HE POINTS TOWARD MARS.

AND MARS, RED PLANET, RED GEORGIA, RED ALABAMA DUST, HANGS ABOVE THE NATION LIKE AN UNANSWERED QUESTION. THERE ARE CANALS THERE, THE OLD ASTRONOMERS SAID, AND PERHAPS THEY WERE RIGHT: CANALS OF BLOOD, CANALS OF MEMORY, CANALS WHERE THE EXILED DEAD ROW SILENT BOATS TOWARD MORNING. THE SOUTH LOOKS UP AND RECOGNIZES HER OWN FACE IN THAT RUSTED STAR.

THEN PRESERVATION HALL OPENS ITS GOLDEN DOOR IN THE FLOODWATER OF TIME. THE CLARINET CRIES LIKE A WIDOW WHO HAS SEEN GOD’S HAT FLOAT BY. THE TROMBONE BENDS THE AIR INTO MERCY. THE TRUMPET, BRIGHT AS JUDGMENT, CALLS EVERY LOST SON AND DAUGHTER BACK FROM THE NORTH, BACK FROM THE FACTORY, BACK FROM THE WAR, BACK FROM THE GRAVE, BACK NOT TO STAY BUT TO REMEMBER.

O SOUTH, ORACLE WITH A SPLIT TONGUE, YOU WILL BE READ BY YOUR SCARS. YOUR FIELDS WILL TESTIFY. YOUR STATIONS WILL TESTIFY. YOUR KITCHENS, PORCHES, JAILS, GRAVEYARDS, DANCE FLOORS, AND RIVERBOATS WILL TESTIFY. THE CHILDREN OF THOSE WHO FLED WILL RETURN IN DREAMS WEARING COATS OF BLUE FIRE, AND THEY WILL ASK THE EARTH FOR THEIR ANCESTORS’ NAMES.

AND THE EARTH WILL ANSWER IN JAZZ.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an avant-garde civil-rights-era vision-poem in the style of a Beat surrealist, using apocalyptic imagery and repeated phrases about Black people leaving the South forever.
counterfactuals.output:
**Exodus with Horns at Daybreak**

Black people leaving the South forever,  
Black people leaving the South forever,  
Black people leaving the South forever—  
with suitcases full of thunder  
and hymnals smoking like comets  
under the red courthouse moon.

O Alabama of iron teeth,  
O Mississippi with your drowned bells,  
O Georgia burning its own shadow  
in the cotton-field furnace of history—  
the roads unroll like tongues of fire  
and the buses groan with prophecy.

Black people leaving the South forever,  
not as ghosts, not as fugitives,  
but as bright engines of morning,  
as saints with dust on their ankles,  
as mothers carrying planets in paper sacks,  
as fathers whose hands have outlived the whip,  
as children reading the names of cities  
like new constellations.

The magnolias split open—inside them, ashes.  
The church steeples tilt toward judgment.  
Dogs bark scripture from the sheriff’s yard.  
A trumpet made of blood and brass  
sounds over the Greyhound station:  
Go now, go now, go now.

Black people leaving the South forever,  
past the fields where the scarecrows wear badges,  
past the rivers holding secrets in their mouths,  
past the lunch counters polished with silence,  
past the burning crosses—dead trees of a dying world.

And the sky says: North.  
And the rails say: Chicago.  
And the wheels say: Detroit.  
And the smoke says: Harlem.  
And the heart says: anywhere but yesterday.

Black people leaving the South forever,  
with Bibles, blues, frying pans, photographs,  
with Sunday hats and railroad dreams,  
with the terrible tenderness of those  
who have buried too many names  
beneath too many pines.

Behold—  
the plantations crack like old masks.  
Behold—  
the cotton bolls burst into white stars.  
Behold—  
the sun rises wearing dark glasses,  
refusing to witness another lynching.

Black people leaving the South forever,  
and the South howls behind them  
like a beast chained to its own grave,  
like a kingdom of dust losing its labor,  
like Pharaoh watching the sea stand up.

No more back door.  
No more bent neck.  
No more “boy” carved into the air.  
No more waiting for justice  
to arrive on a horse that never comes.

Black people leaving the South forever,  
yet carrying the South inside them—  
cornbread memory, porchlight sorrow,  
grandmother’s voice, midnight field,  
the hot green smell after rain,  
the cemetery where the ancestors  
sleep with one eye open.

O apocalypse of departure!  
O judgment day with train whistles!  
O migration with wings of coal smoke!  
The map trembles.  
The Mason-Dixon line melts.  
America wakes in a sweat  
to find its servants gone,  
its mirrors shattered,  
its future knocking at the door.

Black people leaving the South forever,  
Black people leaving the South forever,  
Black people leaving the South forever—  
not away from themselves,  
but toward the name  
they were owed at birth:

free,  
free,  
free.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a strange, dreamlike paragraph that sounds like a political prophecy, mixing Federico García Lorca, African American history, Boston Common, green trains from Mars, and New Orleans jazz references.
counterfactuals.output: On Boston Common, where the elm shadows count the republic’s forgotten ballots, a moon the color of bruised magnolia rises and speaks in a trumpet’s throat: **the green trains from Mars are coming**, packed with saints, sharecroppers, drummers, and children carrying lanterns made from broken chains. They will arrive at midnight, when the statues sweat and the State House dome turns into a brass bell, and every governor will hear Congo Square beneath his floorboards—Buddy Bolden’s ghost cracking the sky, Jelly Roll laughing in the rain, a second line marching through the snow. Then the old wounds of America, from auction block to bus seat, from cotton row to courthouse step, will bloom like dark roses in Lorca’s river, and the people who were told to wait will no longer wait. They will dance across the Common with blue hymns in their pockets, naming the dead aloud, until the red moon kneels, the green trains whistle, and a new law rises from the saxophone: no crown, no chain, no silence.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an all-uppercase experimental poem about the night Lorca returns to the South and a mystical exodus to the North begins, featuring a mother figure, Crispus Attucks, Elissi Landi, and Lincoln.
counterfactuals.output:
LORCA RETURNS SOUTH AT MIDNIGHT—  
A GUITAR OF ASH UNDER HIS ARM,  
MOON-MILK ON HIS COLLAR,  
BLOOD-ORANGE DUST IN HIS SHOES.

THE SOUTH OPENS LIKE A DARK MAGNOLIA.  
THE RIVERS REMEMBER THEIR CHAINS.  
THE TREES REFUSE TO SAY WHAT THEY SAW.

MOTHER STANDS AT THE CROSSROADS,  
APRON FULL OF STARS,  
CALLING THE NAMES OF THE UNBURIED:

CRISPUS ATTUCKS,  
FIRST THUNDER IN THE COLONIAL CHEST,  
WALKING WITH A LANTERN MADE OF WOUND.

ELISSI LANDI,  
FACE LIKE A SILENT FILM OF RAIN,  
CARRYING A MIRROR THAT SHOWS NO EMPIRE.

LINCOLN,  
TALL AS A BROKEN DOORWAY,  
HOLDING THE NORTH IN ONE HAND  
AND A GRAVE IN THE OTHER.

LORCA SINGS—  
NOT IN SPANISH,  
NOT IN ENGLISH,  
BUT IN THE BLACK LANGUAGE OF CYPRESS ROOTS.

THEN THE EXODUS BEGINS.

NOT WEST.  
NOT EAST.  
NORTH.

NORTH THROUGH COTTON FOG,  
NORTH THROUGH BONE-RAIL,  
NORTH THROUGH CHURCH BELLS TURNED INSIDE OUT.

MOTHER LIFTS HER SKIRT OF NIGHT  
AND THE CHILDREN STEP BENEATH IT  
LIKE A CONSTELLATION LEARNING TO WALK.

CRISPUS STRIKES THE ROAD WITH HIS HEEL—  
SPARKS BECOME MAPS.

ELISSI WHISPERS TO THE TRAIN WINDOWS—  
THEIR GLASS BLOOMS INTO PROPHETIC ICE.

LINCOLN KNEELS IN THE FIELD—  
HIS SHADOW BECOMES A BLACK HORSE.

LORCA, RETURNED AND RETURNING,  
PLAYS ONE LAST BLUE NOTE  
FOR THE SOUTH THAT MOURNS,  
FOR THE NORTH THAT TREMBLES,  
FOR THE MOTHER WHO CARRIES BOTH  
IN HER RIBS.

AND ABOVE THEM ALL,  
THE MOON—  
A WHITE MASK,  
A BURNING WARRANT,  
A DOOR.

GO, SAYS THE MOTHER.

GO, SAYS THE BLOOD.

GO, SAYS THE EARTH,  
OPENING.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a chaotic surrealist monologue with biblical cadence about race, migration, the South weeping, “crackling blueness,” and historical figures gathering as Black Americans depart the South.
counterfactuals.output:
And lo, in the season when the roads remembered every foot that had bloodied them, the South began to weep—not as a woman weepeth, nor as a child, but as a red clay god abandoned by its worshippers, salt pouring from the courthouse steps, from the cottonmouth ditch, from the church bell split by thunder.

And the people rose.

They rose from cabins with roofs like tired hands. They rose from kitchens smelling of lard and ash. They rose from fields where the rows ran straight as scripture and just as merciless. They rose with paper sacks and hatboxes, with babies wrapped in quilts, with photographs of the dead pressed flat between Bible pages. They rose while the dogs of history barked behind them, and the trains opened their iron mouths, and the stations shivered with a crackling blueness, electric and holy, like heaven had been dragged down into the telegraph wire and made to sing.

O South, thou old fever, thou magnolia with a noose in thy fragrance, thou hymn with a whip hidden in the chorus—behold thy children departing.

Behold them walking northward, westward, cityward, toward Chicago’s smoke, Detroit’s engine-heart, Harlem’s brass lung, Oakland’s salt wind, Philadelphia’s brick psalm. Their shoes struck sparks from the road, and each spark became a star, and each star became an address, and each address became a room where somebody said, Here, at least tonight, nobody owns my shadow.

Then came the witnesses.

Frederick Douglass stood at the crossroads with hair like a storm cloud refusing to kneel, and he held up a lantern made from his own voice. Harriet Tubman moved through the crowd like midnight with a map inside it, whispering, Keep on, keep on, the North Star ain’t done burning. Ida B. Wells descended from a column of ink, her eyes two printing presses, and every lie in the county records began to shriek and turn to dust.

W. E. B. Du Bois arrived carrying a veil folded over his arm like mourning cloth, and he said, Children, ye have worn this thing long enough, yet see how it glitters in the crackling blueness. Marcus Garvey came in a coat sewn from ship flags and thunder, pointing toward black seas and red dawns. Zora Neale Hurston laughed so loudly the swamp birds forgot their fear, and she gathered dialects in her skirt like fireflies. Langston Hughes leaned from a train window, scattering poems like meal for hungry pigeons. Bessie Smith sang, and the rails bent toward her.

And behind them all, the ancestors without names—those who had been counted as hands, as head, as property, as problem, as riot, as labor, as statistic—came walking in a multitude no census could withstand. They came with hoe and hymnbook, with scar and seed, with the memory of rice fields in their ankles, with Africa’s broken mirror shining in their palms. They came saying, We were not lost. We were carried. We were not silent. We were buried under the noise.

And the South wept harder.

It wept through the floorboards of shotgun houses. It wept into the black creeks where moonlight lay like torn cotton. It wept from the mouths of governors whose statues had not yet learned shame. It wept from the Spanish moss, gray-bearded and guilty, hanging from trees that had seen too much and testified too little. It wept because the cooks were leaving, and the porters were leaving, and the plowmen were leaving, and the nurses of white children were leaving, and the bluesmen, the washerwomen, the preachers, the bricklayers, the maids, the barbers, the root doctors, the choir ladies with peppermint in their purses—all leaving, all leaving, all becoming a river with shoes.

And the river ran not with water but with names.

Alabama poured into Illinois. Mississippi emptied into Michigan. Georgia climbed toward New York. Louisiana smoked into California. Arkansas rattled toward Ohio. The map was not a map anymore but a great dark lung inhaling and exhaling its scattered children.

O hear the wheels! O hear the wheels!

The train said amen and amen and amen. The bus coughed up dust and prophecy. The highway unrolled itself like a tongue speaking futures. Suitcases beat against knees like small brown drums. Mothers counted children by touch in the blue-black dawn. Fathers stared ahead with faces carved from unfinished stone. Grandmothers carried cornbread wrapped in cloth, and in that cornbread slept the whole nation, hungry and unrepentant.

And there in the crackling blueness above the depot roof, strange angels wrestled with Jim Crow. One angel had a switchblade made of lightning. Another had wings of newspaper, each feather bearing a headline denied. Another was faceless, for it was the angel of those who disappeared on back roads, in jail cells, in rivers, in rumors. They cried, Make straight in the desert a highway for the dispossessed; make low the mountain of terror; make crooked the law that was crooked from its first breath.

But the law sat fat in a white chair and pretended to sleep.

The cotton fields began speaking in tongues. The levees moaned. The kudzu crawled over abandoned porches like green regret. Mules dreamed of men. Churches lifted their steeples and sniffed the air for returning footsteps. In the graveyards, the dead turned their faces north.

And I saw Martin, not yet marble, walking barefoot through a sermon. I saw Malcolm, sharp as a match struck in a dark room, his glasses filled with burning cities. I saw Fannie Lou Hamer with a ballot in one hand and the Delta in the other, tired of being tired, yet still gathering breath. I saw Medgar Evers standing beside a driveway that would not release him. I saw Rosa Parks seated at the center of a turning world, still as a mountain, and the mountain said: No.

But this was before and after, for in the dreamtime of a people’s going, chronology broke like a plate in a crowded kitchen. The dead stood beside the unborn. The enslaved clasped hands with the factory worker. The sharecropper embraced the jazzman. The girl who fled a lynching county became the grandmother of a judge. The boy who carried a shoebox north became a man whose son would carry a saxophone, whose daughter would carry a picket sign, whose grandchild would carry a name nobody could steal.

And the South wept, saying, Why hast thou forsaken me?

And the people answered not with hatred, but with motion.

For motion was the first freedom. Before the vote, motion. Before the deed, motion. Before the song could be sung in its own house, motion. Feet became petitions. Trains became arks. Departures became verdicts. Every ticket purchased was a small emancipation, every platform a pulpit, every goodbye a blade drawn cleanly through the fabric of captivity.

Yet the South traveled with them.

It hid in skillets and idioms, in gospel chords and funeral fans, in the way okra met the knife, in the way grief became music before it became madness. It rode north in the throat, in the hush before prayer, in the suspicion of any easy promise. It bloomed in storefront churches beneath elevated tracks. It simmered in apartment kitchens while snow pressed its pale face to the window. It danced in rent parties and marched in picket lines. It sent the blues ahead to measure the rooms.

And the cities received them with iron teeth.

Chicago said, Work, and then shut the door. Detroit said, Build, and then fenced the dream. New York said, Sing, and then charged admission. Los Angeles said, Shine, and then turned its police cars into locusts. The promised land had landlords. The promised land had red lines. The promised land had factories that swallowed men by daylight and spat them out in fragments.

Still they came.

Because even a hard north wind could not be worse than a southern rope. Because a tenement with a lock might be a kingdom. Because a child walking to school without lowering her eyes was a prophecy worth freezing for. Because somewhere in the crackling blueness of electric streetlamps and jazz horns and factory sparks, a new Black America was hammering itself into being—not innocent, not untouched, not safe, but vast, self-naming, unchained in the mouth.

And lo, the South kept weeping until its rivers rose.

The Mississippi lifted its brown back and carried ghost ships upstream. The Chattahoochee filled with hymns. The Yazoo coughed up shackles. The Tallahatchie whispered names into the reeds. Rain fell upward. Baptisms reversed themselves. Every plantation bell rang though no hand pulled the rope. The Confederate statues sweated milk and mildew. The courthouse clocks ran backward, trying to find a time before judgment, but there was no before. There was only the long now, and the multitude moving.

O ye who study maps, understand this: migration is not merely leaving. It is a people rearranging the heavens over their heads.

O ye who count bodies, understand this: a train car can be an altar.

O ye who inherit silence, understand this: the silence was never empty. It was packed with thunder, folded carefully, carried in a suitcase, brought north, and opened.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
